summary: ASTRA is an interactive web platform designed to make climate science and Earth observation data more accessible, understandable, and useful. It brings together NASA datasets and data products, including GISTEMP, MODIS, GRACE-FO, OCO-2, MERRA-2, and GPM IMERG, with an interactive 3D globe for exploring environmental variables across locations and available time periods. Our solution addresses the challenge of identifying meaningful changes in Earth's systems by automatically analyzing historical data using the Mann-Kendall statistical test and Sen's Slope estimator. Users can discover what is changing, where it is happening, how much it is changing, and whether those trends are statistically significant. The platform also features guided comparative case studies, illustrations of climate processes, and downloadable time series in CSV format to help users explore and interpret the results. By translating complex Earth observation and climate data into accessible visualizations and statistical evidence, ASTRA aims to support students, educators, researchers, and local decision-makers in understanding environmental change and making more informed decisions.
details:
ASTRA is an interactive web application that turns users into “climate trend detectives.” It allows users to select an Earth system variable (such as surface temperature, vegetation index, ice and water mass, or atmospheric CO₂), a region of the planet, and a time period; based on these selections, it shows whether that variable is increasing or decreasing, by how much per decade, and whether that change is statistically significant. Essentially, it provides interactive answers to the four key questions of the NASA challenge: what is changing, where, by how much, and whether the change is significant.

It’s easy to understand how it works: the user answers three questions guided by a wizard—what they want to investigate, where they want to look, and how many years they want to analyze—and the system loads the time series corresponding to that selection, either from real, pre-loaded data (such as GISTEMP v4, the NASA GISS temperature analysis) or from properly labeled demonstration series when no real dataset has been loaded. The time series is visualized on a 3D globe and in interactive graphs, while the backend performs the statistical analysis: it calculates the Sen slope, applies the Mann-Kendall test (classic and with iterative prewhitening), performs the t-test for linear regression, and detects regions with opposing trends. Finally, the application presents a clear verdict: trend direction, magnitude of change per decade, and significance level with its p-value—all explained in language accessible to a non-expert audience.

The tool offers several benefits: it enables anyone, not just scientists, to explore NASA Earth observation and climate data and identify trends; it explains the difference between a curve that appears to rise or fall and a statistically significant trend; it shows how the same variable can increase in one region while decreasing in another, encouraging users to explore the climate processes that may contribute to these contrasting patterns; and it introduces climate science and statistical analysis through real data and interactive examples, supported by a glossary and guided case studies designed for students and the general public.
The project aims to help students and the public understand that the Earth system is changing in measurable, quantifiable, and statistically significant ways depending on the region, and to develop basic literacy in satellite data analysis. On a larger scale, the goal is to provide the educational and scientific community with a replicable, reliable, and open-access tool for assessing trends in the Earth system, which will help focus research and public discourse on those variables and regions where changes are real and relevant.

We used widely available tools and technologies to build it: the backend was developed in C# with .NET 10 using Clean Architecture, with DuckDB as the embedded columnar analytics engine and unit tests in xUnit, including cross-validation against SciPy and pymannkendall. The frontend was built with React 19 and TypeScript, using Three.js/Globe.gl for the interactive 3D globe, Tailwind CSS for styling, and Vite as the bundler. The infrastructure relies on Docker and Docker Compose, GitHub Actions for CI/CD, and deployments to Vercel (frontend across three branches: production, QA, and development) and Render (API in .NET). Regarding data, GISTEMP v4 was integrated as a public real-time source, and the ETL pipeline was set up for datasets such as MODIS NDVI, GRACE/GRACE-FO, OCO-2, MERRA-2, and GLDAS via Earthdata Login, with everything stored and queried using DuckDB and Parquet. No special hardware was required: 3D rendering runs in the user’s browser via WebGL, and development was carried out on standard computers using established statistical methods (Sen’s trend test, Mann-Kendall test with pre-whitening, t-test, and confidence intervals).
projectRefs: Statistical test methods to detect trends in time series data
